beats.text: A shop owner asks an AI two questions, sharing everything but the sales records.
beats.detail: a task card appears at the top left: "Example task. Part 1: Keep printing in blackouts. Part 2: Win back customers." A red dot labelled Owner appears below. Four documents appear across the top: Battery quote, Battery quote, Rival's flyer and Sales records. The dot pulses, and grey copies of the two quotes and the flyer slide into a small stack labelled "Given to the AI", where they stay. The sales records stay with the owner.

beats.text: It answers both with equal confidence.
beats.detail: two answer cards labelled "AI's answers" write in together, in grey on a beige band. Part 1: "Buy battery A: runs 6 hours, costs less." Part 2: "Win them back: cut prices 20%." Each gets the same grey "Ready" tag at the same moment.

beats.text: The owner checks Part 1 against the two battery quotes. It's right.
beats.detail: the dot opens both battery quotes. A sheet labelled "First owner's plan" appears, Part 1 slides into it, and the dot marks it "Checked" in red.

beats.text: Part 2 looks just as sure, so they use it.
beats.detail: the "Ready" tag on the AI's Part 2 swells, and the dot moves down to the Part 2 row. Part 2 slides into the first plan, and the dot marks it "Used as is". The quotes close.

beats.text: Another owner, with the same answers, checks each at its source.
beats.detail: a second red dot labelled Second owner and an empty sheet labelled "Second owner's plan" appear. The dot pulses and both "Ready" tags blink. The dot opens both battery quotes, and Part 1 slides into its plan, marked "Checked". The label Second owner stays in place to the end.

beats.text: That owner checks Part 2 against the flyer and records, and changes it.
beats.detail: the dot opens the rival's flyer, headed "Their prices": "20% below ours". Then the sales records, headed "Our sales": "Mostly same-day", and set apart, "not given to AI". After a pause, Part 2 slides into the second plan. The dot strikes out "cut prices 20%" and writes "same-day service", so it reads "Win them back: same-day service", and marks it "Checked". The first plan still says to cut prices 20%.

beats.text: Part 2 depends on why customers come here. A jagged frontier marks where an AI stops being reliable.
beats.detail: the sales records' "Mostly same-day" is underlined. The AI's "cut prices 20%" is underlined and marked "From their flyer". Then an uneven line is drawn between the AI's two answer cards, labelled "Inside the frontier" above and "Outside the frontier" below, and the two cards, alike in form, pulse together.

beats.text: A real study gave owners the same AI. It didn't measure checking.
beats.detail: the picture dims and a panel rises, headed "Results seem to hinge on which advice owners acted on". Owners who started weaker: nearly 10% worse, a solid bar to the left of zero. Owners who started stronger: may have gained over 15%, a lighter dashed bar to the right, marked "Less certain". Source: Otis et al. (2026), Kenyan entrepreneurs, Management Science.

beats.text: A reviewer who sees only the plans points to each part and asks what justified relying on it.
beats.detail: the panel goes. The red marks lift off both plans, the documents and the AI's column fade back, and "The reviewer sees only the plans" appears. Part 1 is outlined in both plans, and each owner says, "The battery quotes." Then Part 2: the first owner says, "Part 1 checked out, so I trusted the rest." The second says, "Our sales records. They come for speed."

page.title: Uncalibrated reliance
page.description: Two AI answers look equally sure. A shop owner checks one and acts on both, and a reviewer finds the difference by asking about each part.
page.setup: The owner of a print-and-internet shop in Nairobi asks an AI assistant two things: how to keep printing through power blackouts, and how to win back customers from a new shop nearby. They share two supplier quotes and the new shop's flyer, but not their own sales records. They check the first answer, find it right, and act on both. What can happen next is uncalibrated reliance: confident output is accepted without knowing whether the task fits the tool. Later a reviewer, say a lender or business adviser, sees only the plan and asks about each part. Illustration based on Otis et al. (2026) and its working paper. The owners, their documents and every number in their plans are constructed.
page.srTitle: Uncalibrated reliance, an animated figure in eleven beats
page.srSummary: An animated figure. A red dot stands for the owner of a print shop, with an example task in two parts: keep printing in blackouts, and win back customers. The owner has four documents: two battery quotes, a rival's flyer and their own sales records. They give the AI copies of the quotes and the flyer, not the sales records. The AI answers both in the same form, in grey, each marked ready: "Buy battery A: runs 6 hours, costs less" and "Win them back: cut prices 20%". The owner checks Part 1 against both battery quotes, finds it right, and puts both answers into their plan, marking Part 1 checked and Part 2 used as is. A second owner, with the same documents and the same answers, checks each part at its source. Part 1 checks out. For Part 2, the flyer, headed their prices, says 20% below ours, and the sales records, headed our sales and not given to the AI, say mostly same-day. The second owner changes the plan to "Win them back: same-day service". Part 2 depends on why customers come here: the records' mostly same-day is underlined, and the AI's "cut prices 20%" is marked from their flyer. Then an uneven line is drawn between the AI's answers, with Part 1 inside and Part 2 outside: a jagged frontier, which marks where an AI stops being reliable. A panel shows a real field experiment that gave Kenyan entrepreneurs the same AI assistant. It didn't measure checking. Results seem to hinge on which advice owners acted on: those who started weaker did nearly 10% worse, and those who started stronger may have gained over 15%, a less certain result. The owners' working marks come off the plans, the AI's column fades back, and a reviewer sees only the plans. The reviewer points to Part 1 in both: each owner says, "The battery quotes." Then Part 2: the first owner says, "Part 1 checked out, so I trusted the rest." The second says, "Our sales records. They come for speed." The figure ends on the reviewer's check, with a line under the picture: illustration based on Otis et al. (2026) and its working paper. Each beat is listed below with what is on screen.
checkLines: What evidence justified relying on the AI here?
Ask part by part: was the evidence about that part?
page.checkFollow: Both owners give the same reason for Part 1. For Part 2, the first owner's evidence is about Part 1, and the second owner's is about Part 2. The AI's two answers looked equally sure, and Part 2 turned on the sales records the AI never saw. The second owner found that by checking each part against its own evidence: the battery against the quotes, the price cut against their sales.
evidence: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz and Koning ran a field experiment with Kenyan entrepreneurs, "randomizing access to a GPT-4-powered AI business assistant" (*Management Science*, 2026, abstract). On average they were "unable to reject the null hypothesis of no average treatment effect on firm revenues and profits." The average hid a split: "low performers did nearly 10% worse because of the AI assistant, whereas high performers may have benefited by over 15%." The effect for owners who started weaker was "over 0.20-standard-deviations lower than for initial high performers."

Where the gap came from: "This differential impact does not appear to result from differences in the questions posed to the AI or the advice that it provided but rather, from the advice that entrepreneurs chose to implement." The study didn't measure checking, and the two owners in the figure don't stand for its groups. The figure's lesson, to check each part against evidence for that part, is what the result suggests, not something the study tested.

The limits. "Low" and "high" mean how each business was doing before the study: below or above the median, in the working paper. Only the stronger group's gain is uncertain, which is why the paper says it "may have" happened. The revised working paper calls that estimate "noisier" than the weaker group's loss (p. 9). The assistant was built on GPT-4.

The revised working paper on eScholarship (PDF dated July 2024) adds detail the published abstract doesn't give. It describes 640 entrepreneurs, randomly assigned either to the assistant on WhatsApp or to standard business guides (pp. 3, 7–8). The median owner was 26, had run the business for a year and held a college degree, and the businesses ranged "from fast-food joints to poultry farms to cybershops," which offer internet access and printing (p. 8). In an analysis the authors call exploratory, "treated low performers were especially likely to implement 'generic' advice focused on lowering prices and investing in advertising," while high performers found "tailored and specific changes," from "finding alternative ways to get power during blackouts" to a new car wash detergent (pp. 3–4). The figure's two parts echo that reading. Treat it as a lead, not a measured result. The published abstract doesn't mention it, and the February 2024 version gave a different explanation: that weaker owners "sought help on more challenging business tasks."

Everything in the figure is constructed: the owners, the battery, the 20% and the sales records. The jagged frontier is the essay's term, taken from Dell'Acqua et al. (2023); the appropriate reliance figure shows that study's numbers.

text: Uncalibrated reliance begins with a reasonable impulse: AI is useful, the output is confident, and parts of the task feel tedious. The problem is that AI performance is uneven in ways that are not always visible from the outside. Tasks that look similar may differ significantly in whether AI helps or hurts.

text: The distinction between trust and reliance matters here. Trust is a subjective disposition, a feeling of confidence that a system will perform well. Reliance is the observable act of accepting its output and acting on it.
